source.title: SpeechGPT-Gen: Scaling Chain-of-Information Speech Generation
source.authors: Dong Zhang; Xin Zhang; Jun Zhan; Shi-Min Li; Yaqian Zhou; Xi-Peng Qiu

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Extends model-size scaling experiments to speech flow-matching models and reports downstream performance across model sizes, but does not test the claimed language-model power laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. as background, but does not fit or test power laws for held-out language-model loss or compute-optimal allocation. Its speech-model training-loss and downstream scaling results are recorded; the training-loss findings do not measure any listed version's specified power-law behavior.
record.test_reason: This is a speech-generation method paper. It cites Kaplan et al. only as motivation. Its Section 5.3 'scalability' check compares three flow-matching speech model sizes (300M, 600M, 1.2B). It reports qualitative trends only: no values, no power-law fit, no extrapolation, no compute allocation, and no predictive relation to loss. Three monotone points from a non-language-model speech decoder cannot show whether any version's power-law or 'predictable' claim holds. V5 would need a power-law form, and V6 names predictable downstream scaling, which this does not establish.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right for Section 5.3, but incomplete. The paper's main conclusion is that Chain-of-Information Generation, which decouples semantic and perceptual modeling, together with a semantic prior for flow matching, gives superior and more efficient zero-shot TTS, voice conversion and speech-to-speech dialogue. The scaling claim is secondary: larger flow-matching models and more tokens show 'excellent scalability'. There is no power-law claim.
record.recipe_differences: Speech flow-matching model-size and token-count scaling, rather than held-out language-model cross-entropy power-law fitting or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary with model size and number of training tokens. The downstream comparison fixes ODE steps at 8.

fits_no_version.finding: Flow-matching speech models of 300M, 600M and 1.2B parameters, scaled by depth only, show training loss falling with tokens seen, and falling faster for larger models (Figure 6 left).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Speech flow-matching training loss falls with data and model size; no power-law form is established.

fits_no_version.finding: On VCTK zero-shot voice conversion (8 ODE steps), WER falls and speaker similarity rises monotonically across the three model sizes. This is figure only, with no fit (Figure 6 right).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream speech-generation quality improves monotonically with flow-matching model size over a 4x range.

record.problems: The scaling plots provide no numerical curve values in the text, and no uncertainty estimates are reported. The loss result is training loss for speech flow-matching models, not held-out language-model cross-entropy; no power-law fits or extrapolation tests are reported.

untested.parts: No language-model held-out loss sweep and no power-law fit.
No fit on small runs and no extrapolation.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count; sizes vary by depth only.
Speech models are studied, but no power-law form is fitted or tested, and the loss reported is training loss only.
There is no predictive relation between scale or loss and downstream metrics; only a three-point qualitative trend in speech models.
No examination of fitting choices or exponents.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'supports V6' label is dropped, because three qualitative points from a speech decoder do not test predictable downstream scaling of language models. Table 3 lists 16 heads while Section 4.1 says 8 heads. Section 4.1 mentions only the Base and Large sizes. The size sweep varies depth only (6, 12 and 24 layers at width 1024), so model size is confounded with depth.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining cross-entropy sweep for language models; no power-law fit in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fit or prediction of much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation experiment or parameter/token allocation fit.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
Although speech models are studied, the paper does not test whether a power-law form holds across modalities or training regimes; its reported training loss is not held-out pretraining loss.
Tests WER and speaker similarity for speech generation across flow-matching model sizes, not language-model downstream tasks or a quantitative predictive relationship with pretraining loss.
No study of fit choices, exponents, disagreements between scaling-law setups, or curve bending.
